title: Discrete Adjoint Schrödinger Bridge Sampler
one_liner: Learn a discrete sampler by treating generation as a controlled random jump process from a source distribution to a target distribution and training the control with adjoint matching.
lead: Many modern samplers generate continuous values, but many real targets are discrete: symbols, categories, text pieces, or molecular choices. In discrete spaces, small perturbations do not produce usable derivatives, so methods that rely on smooth motion in continuous space do not transfer directly. This paper extends the Schrödinger bridge view of sampling to discrete state spaces. A Schrödinger bridge is a minimum-control path problem: start from a simple source distribution, meaning a weighted set of starting states, end at the target distribution, meaning a weighted set of desired final states, and pay as little control cost as possible along the way. The paper shows that the core adjoint matching idea does not depend on continuous coordinates. Under a cyclic group structure, meaning each discrete coordinate supports wrap-around addition within a finite set, the method can define reference jumps, learn control ratios, and alternate between a controller and a corrector to produce target samples with lower training cost than many discrete samplers.

problem.h2: Why discrete sampling is harder than continuous sampling
paras: In continuous spaces, many sampler-training methods can ask how the output changes under a tiny movement. In discrete spaces, there is no smaller version of changing one category into another. A method therefore needs a different way to describe motion from simple samples to target samples.

The Schrödinger bridge formulation gives that description by turning sampling into path control. Instead of learning one direct jump from source to target, it learns how the probability of discrete jumps should change over time so that the whole random process ends at the target distribution with low control cost.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Build a discrete random jump process with the right algebraic structure, then learn the bridge control by adjoint matching rather than by expensive pathwise optimization.

panels.title: 1. Start from an easy discrete source
panels.viz_args: Begin with a simple random distribution over discrete states that can be sampled cheaply.
panels.caption: The source distribution is easy to draw from but does not match the target.

panels.title: 2. Add reference jumps
panels.caption: A reference jump process defines how states would evolve without learned control.

panels.title: 3. Learn controller and corrector
panels.viz_args: One network adjusts jump tendencies during the path; another network enforces the final target relation.
panels.caption: The controller shapes the path and the corrector anchors the end distribution.

panels.title: 4. Alternate adjoint updates
panels.caption: Training switches between updating path control and updating target correction so each part supervises the other.

panels.title: 5. Sample from the learned bridge
panels.caption: The final process produces discrete samples that follow the target distribution more closely than the uncontrolled reference process.

steps.text: Define a continuous-time Markov chain, meaning a random process that jumps between discrete states over time, with simple reference jump rates that are easy to simulate.

steps.b: Impose a cyclic group state structure
steps.text: Represent the state space so additions and differences stay inside the finite discrete set, because adjoint matching needs a consistent way to describe how one state changes into another under reference jumps.
Train a model that changes the reference jump tendencies over time so the path gradually bends toward the target instead of wandering under the uncontrolled process.
Train a terminal correction model that ties the end of the path to the target distribution, because the controller alone can shape trajectories but still miss the exact final mass allocation.

steps.b: Alternate the two updates and sample
steps.text: Update controller and corrector in turn, then run the learned jump process with time discretization to generate target samples.

paras: The paper changes where adjoint matching can be used. It shows that the core training idea can be reformulated for discrete jump processes, provided the state space and reference process are chosen so the needed ratios and shifted states remain well defined.
object.object: controlled discrete jump process that bridges source samples to target samples

hidden.name: the optimal time-varying jump adjustment that turns the reference process into the target-reaching bridge
paras: The sampler never observes this ideal control directly. It only sees source samples, target samples, and simulated paths under the current model. The hidden quantity is the jump adjustment that would make every intermediate move contribute to the right final target mass.

In discrete spaces this quantity is subtle because moving probability mass is about changing jump rates, not sliding points through coordinates. The controller and corrector split that job: one shapes the path law over time, and the other enforces the terminal relation to the target.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark the parts of the bridge that the method must model well in order to generate correct discrete samples.

reads.html: Ask how the random jump process should change at each time so simple starting samples end up distributed like the target samples.
DASBS learns the control that reweights reference jump paths into a Schrödinger bridge, with a controller for path shaping and a corrector for terminal consistency.

mechanism.h2: Why the discrete bridge construction works
paras: The reference process matters because it provides a baseline law over paths that is easy to simulate. The bridge then only has to learn how to tilt that law toward the target, not how to invent a path process from nothing.

The cyclic group structure matters because the method repeatedly compares a state with a shifted version of the same state. Those comparisons must stay inside the same finite state space or the required ratios are undefined. The wrap-around algebra gives a closed update rule for those shifted states.

Alternating controller and corrector updates matter because the bridge has two responsibilities. The path must move in sensible directions at intermediate times, and the final time must match the target distribution. If the method trains only the controller, the endpoint can drift. If it trains only the terminal correction, the intermediate path can become inefficient or unstable.

stages.s: Simple source samples and target discrete samples
Run a reference random jump process on a cyclic discrete state space
Learn controller and corrector with adjoint matching
Alternate updates until bridge paths align with the target

math.words: find jump control that reaches the target while paying small deviation cost from the reference process
math.equation: min_u  E[ integral control_cost(u_t, X_t) dt + terminal_cost(X_1) ]
symbols: the time-varying control that changes jump tendencies at time t
the discrete state at time t along the random jump path
the penalty for deviating from the reference jump process
the penalty that enforces agreement with the target distribution at the final time

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the reference chain jumps left or right with equal rate, but the target puts much more mass on states near the right side.
A learned controller increases rightward jump rates early in the path and decreases them later when enough mass has already moved.
If the controller pushes too hard, the control cost rises.
If it pushes too weakly, the terminal cost rises because the endpoint misses the target distribution.
Training searches for a balance where the target is reached without using unnecessarily strong jump distortions.

math.note: The discrete bridge view turns sampling into a controlled path problem, so the sampler is learned through path-cost tradeoffs rather than direct one-step prediction alone.

charts.title: Heavier discrete sampler training
charts.note: Methods that optimize discrete samplers without this bridge structure can spend more computation on learning path behavior that the reference process already provides.

charts.title: DASBS
charts.note: The gains come from reusing a simple reference jump law and learning only the control needed to turn that law into the target-reaching bridge.

items.b: The state space may not fit the required algebra.
items.html: If the discrete variables cannot be represented with the needed wrap-around structure, the shifted-state comparisons used by adjoint matching become hard to define cleanly.

items.b: The reference process may mix too slowly or too quickly.
items.html: A very weak reference process fails to explore enough states, while a very strong one erases useful structure and forces the controller to undo too much random motion.

items.b: Alternating updates can fall out of sync.
items.html: If the controller is much stronger than the corrector, or the other way around, one part may train on stale supervision from the other part because the alternating updates assume both components improve on a similar timescale.

Choose a reference jump law with good coverage, verify that the state encoding supports the required shifted-state operations, and balance the controller and corrector update schedule so both parts improve together because each component supplies supervision that the other component immediately reuses.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Use a small discrete target such as categorical sequences or binary strings with known target probabilities. Compare uncontrolled reference sampling, a simpler discrete diffusion baseline, and DASBS.

Visualize the evolving state histograms over time and measure final distribution error. The demo should show that DASBS works because it learns how to reshape the whole jump process, not because it memorizes terminal states without controlling the path.
demo.closing: A convincing result is that the learned bridge moves mass toward the right target regions early enough that the final histogram aligns well with the target while training cost stays moderate.
